readings.title: Reading a household energy chart
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
Residents received a monthly electricity chart. A high winter bar worried one family, although the chart did not show temperature or occupancy. The main obstacle was a comparison without household context. Relatives had stayed for two weeks, and heating needs differed from the previous month. At first, the people involved did not agree on which part of the proposal deserved the most attention.

To investigate, the team used a review of usage alongside daily notes. Advisers compared bills with weather and time at home while protecting private details. The organizers kept the first stage small enough to change without wasting substantial time or resources.

The evidence indicated the chart alone could not explain the rise. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a guide to interpreting changes before taking action. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. The records were useful because they described ordinary use rather than an ideal situation imagined at a meeting.

The case suggests a broader point: energy data needs a fair point of comparison. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The group published its reasons so that people who preferred a different result could still understand the choice. For those taking part in reading a household energy chart, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records.

readings.title: Choosing lights for a shared hallway
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
An apartment committee considered lights that respond to movement. Residents liked the saving idea but feared a dark hallway between sensors. The main obstacle was coverage gaps near the stair landing. The first proposal placed sensors according to a floor plan rather than actual walking routes. The question mattered to people with different schedules and levels of experience, so one account could not represent everyone.

To investigate, the team used an evening walk with temporary markers. Residents traced common paths and checked how long the lights stayed on. A simple record of what happened each day gave the team a starting point for comparison.

The evidence indicated one extra sensor improved continuous visibility. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced revised sensor positions and a safe override. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Some participants welcomed the change immediately, while others noticed practical details that needed further work.

The case suggests a broader point: efficiency should not weaken everyday safety. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The result was a revised plan, not a claim that every difficulty had disappeared. For those taking part in choosing lights for a shared hallway, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: A library window in summer
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A library closed blinds all day to keep its rooms cool. Readers complained that the morning area became unnecessarily dark. The main obstacle was one shading rule for changing sunlight. The sunny side moved across the building, but staff followed a fixed opening checklist. The initial idea sounded reasonable, yet the details of the place made it harder to carry out than expected.

To investigate, the team used temperature and light observations by hour. The team noted room use and consulted building staff on safe ventilation. Instead of relying on a single opinion, the team invited several users to describe what they actually did.

The evidence indicated timed shading maintained comfort and light. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a room-by-room schedule for blinds. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. This allowed the organizers to separate a temporary inconvenience from a pattern that required attention.

The case suggests a broader point: small energy choices benefit from timing. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. They also decided when to check the arrangement again, because conditions could change over time. For those taking part in a library window in summer, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Explaining a community solar proposal
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A neighbourhood group discussed solar panels for a shared building. The first leaflet showed expected savings but omitted maintenance responsibilities. The main obstacle was benefits described without ongoing duties. Residents could not judge who would inspect equipment or pay for future repairs. The people affected were invited to comment before a permanent arrangement was chosen.

To investigate, the team used a full-cost discussion with specialists. The committee listed installation, maintenance and ownership questions in plain language. The first trial produced both useful results and questions the team could not yet answer.

The evidence indicated clear responsibilities improved the discussion. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a revised proposal showing both costs and benefits. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Rather than hide those limits, the public note explained how the next version had been selected.

The case suggests a broader point: an energy choice needs a complete picture. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. That explanation made later changes easier to discuss with residents and staff. For those taking part in explaining a community solar proposal, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
When a community changes the household energy advice programme, a short explanation can be as important as the change itself. People want to know what problem was noticed, how information was gathered and why one option was selected. For a project about household energy and practical choices, staff observed actual use rather than relying only on a drawing or an early promise. The evidence revealed an obstacle that was not obvious at first. Organizers made a limited adjustment and told residents when it would be reviewed. They also described the limits of the trial, because a small number of visits cannot represent every future situation. An honest account made the decision easier to question and improve.

translation.referenceAnswer: 社区调整一项服务时，简短解释可能和改动本身同样重要。人们想知道发现了什么问题、如何收集信息，以及为何选择某个方案。在一个有关家庭节能与能源选择的项目中，工作人员观察实际使用，而不只依靠图纸或最初的承诺。证据揭示了起初并不明显的障碍。组织者作出有限调整，并告知居民何时重新评估。他们也说明试行的局限，因为少量使用经历不能代表未来所有情况。诚实的说明让这项决定更容易被讨论和改进。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to the local energy team suggesting a practical change to the household energy advice programme. Describe who should be consulted, how the change could be tried, and when it should be reviewed.
writing.explanation: 范文供考生自评，注意任务要点、组织结构及语言准确性。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Committee Members,
I would like to propose a small improvement to the household energy advice programme. People have noticed a comparison without household context, and a short trial could help us understand how often this problem occurs. We should ask regular users and people who have not used the service before to describe their experiences. Their comments may reveal details that a plan made in an office would miss.
For one month, staff could keep a simple record of participation, time spent and any difficulties reported. We should also explain the purpose of the trial in clear language so that residents know how to contribute. After the month, please publish a brief summary of both benefits and limits. The final decision should be based on what people actually experienced, with a date for checking the arrangement again.
Yours sincerely,
A resident
